## Why a second article

In a [previous article](../2026-05-10_coach_ai/index.qmd) I described the first 
stable version of the coaching
workflow: normalized planning context, persistent prompts, structured output,
validation, and targeted repair.

That design worked, but it still behaved more like an engineering pipeline
than like an application.

The system could generate useful weekly reviews and plans, but the workflow
was still heavily shaped by the implementation itself. The user experience was
non-existent (termial only), the tool was not portable (I could only run it 
from my computer), state was spread across a few operational layers 
(Notion, intervals.icu, local files) with no clear single source of truth.

So I made some changes.

The main shift is not that the model became smarter. Fine tuning would still be
a good thing to do, but there is a lot more to gain by working on
the surrounding software and make it more explicit.

The workflow now has:

- a dedicated UI rather than a mostly script-like interaction model
- explicit form validation and state checks before generation is triggered
- durable storage in Google Cloud Storage as the system of record
- Cloud Run deployment as a stable runtime surface
- retrieval-backed prompting through an OpenAI vector store (RAG)
- usage logging for observability
- race-aware weekly review against athlete-defined race objectives
- a structured workout-template library that the planner now selects and
  adapts deterministically before any targeted repair fallback is considered

This article focuses on these changes. 

## What changed architecturally

### The system boundary became clearer

The earlier version used Notion as both an operational data layer and a major
interaction surface: I was saving data directly in there, and displaying outputs.

That was useful for getting the first version working quickly, but it bundled
too many responsibilities into one tool. It meant the system was partly an
application and partly a collection of synchronized tables. The result was an 
instable, hard to replicate, and difficult to version system. Having such a heavy 
dependency on a tool like Notion would also make it difficult to market the
solution, if that was in scope.

The current design is more opinionated:

- `GCS` is now the system of record
- `Notion` is not really used anymore. It is still linked to the workflow as a 
  secondary target to save the planned week, but that is only for my own conveniance: 
  Notion synchs with Google Calendar so I can quickly see which sessions I have
  planned for the day
- `intervals.icu` provides executed workouts, wellness, and thresholds
- `OpenAI` handles generation
- the Dash app is now the primary user interface

That is a much better fit for a controlled software workflow.

The high-level architecture now looks like this:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    CR[Cloud Run<br/>Dash app]
    MU[Monitoring app]
    GCS[(Google Cloud Storage)]
    BQ[(BigQuery billing export)]
    OA[OpenAI API<br/>generation + vector store retrieval]
    ICU[Intervals.icu API]
    NOTION[Notion]
    SM[Secret Manager]
    
    SM --> CR
    SM --> MU
    CR <--> OA
    CR <--> ICU
    CR <--> GCS
    CR --> NOTION
    GCS --> MU
    BQ --> MU

    style CR fill:#dff3ea,stroke:#1f6f4a,stroke-width:3px,color:#123524
    style MU fill:#dff3ea,stroke:#1f6f4a,stroke-width:3px,color:#123524
```

The important architectural choice is that the Dash application is now the
orchestrator and GCS is the system of record.

The monitoring app is a read-only surface. It reads telemetry logs from GCS and
infrastructure cost data from the Cloud Billing export in BigQuery. It does not
create a second operational data store of its own.

### The app orchestrates the workflow

The UI does not simply replace command-line steps with buttons. It introduces a
different control model.

The app now exposes distinct components for:

- season planning
- zones review
- weekly plan generation and editing
- weekly review synchronization and coach review generation

## Why the UI matters

### Validation moved earlier in the workflow

One of the biggest improvements is that more checks now happen before an LLM
request is even sent.

For example, the season-planning interface validates required fields, date
format, and race placement before generation is allowed. That
is a simple point, but an important one. If the input form already knows the
season start is after the season end, there is no reason to spend tokens
discovering that downstream.

The weekly workflow benefits from the same idea. Before a plan is generated, 
the app already knows:

- which season is active
- which week is being planned
- what session-availability slots exist for that week
- what saved state already exists in storage
- whether race-day rows need to be injected from the season calendar

That allows the generation step to start from a better-defined state.

`TODO: insert screenshot of the week plan editor with availability rows and the generated week plan table`

Under the hood, that flow now looks like this:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[User selects week + availability] --> B[Availability validation]
    B --> C[Build planning context from season + zones + prior reviews + races]
    C --> D[Inject race-week context]
    D --> E[Surface structured template candidates]
    E --> F[Retrieve coaching evidence from vector store]
    F --> G[OpenAI generates session intents]
    G --> H[Deterministic template selection + adaptation]
    H --> I[Deterministic normalization + validation + load scoring + race-day row injection]
    I --> J{Valid?}
    J -- No --> K[Deterministic targeted repair]
    K --> L{Still invalid?}
    L -- Yes --> M[Targeted LLM repair for rejected sessions or dates]
    L -- No --> N[User edits plan]
    M --> I
    J -- Yes --> N[User edits plan]
    N --> O[Save week plan to GCS]
    O --> P[Sync saved week plan to Notion]
```

Another rule now lives in this deterministic layer: session load is no longer
trusted as an LLM-produced scalar. The app recalculates the authoritative
Swim, Bike, and Run load from `Prescription Structure` using a Joe Friel /
TrainingPeaks style `duration × intensity² × 100` rule. That makes load a
software policy rather than a probabilistic guess.

The availability model also became more granular. The earlier UI used one row
per day, which was too coarse for common cases like "30 minutes to run before
work, but 60 minutes available to swim later." The current app instead stores
availability as one row per session slot. That allows the planner and
validator to respect different duration caps for different sports on the same
date, and it allows a single Bike+Run slot to be treated as a possible brick
window rather than as two unrelated single-sport permissions. It also means
free-text slot notes can now be upgraded into real constraints when the note is
clear enough. For example, a note like "Bike should be at least 1h45min" is no
longer just prompt flavor; it becomes a validator-enforced minimum for the bike
work that uses that slot.

The weekly planner itself has also become stricter. The LLM is no longer asked
to draft the full week first. It now proposes `session intents` such as sport,
goal, brick status, purpose, target duration, and for Swim sessions a separate
technique-emphasis signal. Code then selects from a
structured Swim/Bike/Run template catalog, adapts the chosen template
deterministically, resolves numeric target ranges from saved athlete anchors,
recalculates duration and load, and validates the result. The same
deterministic layer also fixes a subset of obvious plan defects in code, such
as mismatched planned duration, overlong time-based strength or brick
segments, and small brick-over-day-cap overruns, before escalating anything
back to the LLM. The next repair step is still deterministic: rejected
sessions are patched in place where possible, or re-materialized from another
structured template if the original choice was poor. LLM repair is now the
last stage, and it only sees the rejected sessions or dates rather than the
whole week.

That stricter deterministic layer now also protects against two easy failure
modes that showed up in earlier iterations. First, the selector no longer
accepts semantically incompatible templates just because the duration is close,
so a non-brick threshold bike intent should not quietly turn into a brick-prep
ride. Second, pool swims must retain real structure. A single continuous
`Main 50:00` style swim block is treated as invalid; the planner expects
warmup, main work, cooldown, and where appropriate some explicit drill content.
And at the wording layer, unresolved alternatives should not survive into the
final rows. If the planner chooses a long run, the saved row should not still
say "long run or test unless ..." after the other option has already been
discarded.

This is a more opinionated architecture than the earlier library-assisted
prompting approach. The model still matters, but it now operates one level
higher in the stack. Its main planning job is to choose and justify the right
session intent; the software is increasingly responsible for the workout
structure itself.

The structured catalog is also broader now than it was in the first template
pass. In addition to the hand-authored core families, the current `Your Best
Triathlon` workout subset has been converted into machine-adaptable structured
templates, with brick workouts split into executable Bike and Run segments so
they can move through the same deterministic selector and validator.

That separation matters for swim design in particular. Technique focus is no
longer treated as a synonym for "make this a drill-only swim." Most swims can
now stay endurance or threshold sessions while still carrying a small explicit
drill component in the warmup or early set.

### Editing became explicit rather than accidental

In the earlier workflow, I was editing several tables and scripts directly to
provide inputs.

The UI makes these intervention points explicit:

- edit season inputs, then generate a preview
- inspect the preview, then confirm and persist it
- generate a weekly plan, review the rows, then save
- sync the review week from Intervals.icu, add feedback, and then ask for a
  weekly coach review
- open a single completed workout and request a session-specific review only
  when needed

This is a better human-in-the-loop design.

The human is not asked to supervise the model at every token. The human is
asked to supervise state transitions where judgment is actually useful:
confirming a season, editing a plan, adding subjective feedback, or deciding
whether an individual workout deserves deeper inspection.

That pattern starts with season creation itself.

`TODO: insert screenshot of the season planner form including the race table and preview/confirm flow`

The season workflow is deliberately staged:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[User enters season inputs] --> B[UI validation]
    B --> C[Build deterministic season context<br/>recent fitness + threshold anchors + race specs]
    C --> D[Retrieve coaching evidence from vector store]
    D --> E[OpenAI preflight<br/>Do I have enough context?]
    E --> F{Questions needed?}
    F -- Yes --> G[Show up to 5 targeted questions in UI]
    G --> H[User answers once]
    H --> I[OpenAI final season planning pass]
    F -- No --> I
    I --> J[Render final preview in app]
    J --> K[Coach edits race strategy, block targets, CTL/Form seeds deterministically]
    K --> L{User confirms?}
    L -- No --> M[Reset or regenerate]
    L -- Yes --> N[Persist artifacts + tables to GCS]
    N --> O[Active season available to rest of app]
```

Two design details matter here.

First, the season form no longer asks for a manual end date. The app derives
season end as the Sunday of the week containing the last planned race, and it
blocks plans longer than 365 days. That turns a fuzzy user input into a
deterministic software rule.

Second, the season workflow is now explicitly question-first rather than
draft-first. The preflight pass receives everything the software can assemble
automatically: current CTL and ATL when available, recent 4-6 week training
summaries from stored data, threshold anchors from saved zones, and standard
race specs that are normalized in code instead of guessed by the model. If the
coach still wants clarification, those questions are shown directly to the
user before any season draft is produced. The answers are then passed into one
final planning pass, after which no additional clarification loop is allowed.

The preview is also more useful than it was when I first wrote this article.
Once the season is generated, some edits are now deterministic rather than
regenerative. The coach can adjust taper and recovery days in the race table,
edit block-level targets and `duration_weeks`, seed starting CTL and Form, and
see the chart update immediately. The software recalculates the timeline,
projected weekly load, CTL, and Form without calling the LLM again, and a
reset action restores the untouched generated draft if the manual edits go in a
bad direction.

### Review and feedback became first-class workflow objects

The current system now treats weekly review and single-workout feedback as
separate product surfaces, not as incidental text outputs.

That distinction matters.

A weekly review is a synthesis artifact across a whole week of planned and
executed work. A single-workout review is different. It is much narrower and
uses execution details plus athlete feedback to interpret one completed swim,
bike, or run session.

It also improves cost and control. The app generates single-session reviews on
demand, rather than precomputing commentary for every row whether it is needed
or not. That keeps the expensive reasoning surface narrow and tied to a user
action.

Race review has also become more explicit. When the selected week contains a
race, weekly review now switches into a race-aware mode. Instead of treating
the week as a failed taper or an underloaded training microcycle, the system
uses the athlete's saved race objectives and evaluates the event against those
objectives. The review still comments on the individual swim, bike, and run
segments, but it also produces a whole-event `overall_race_review`, which is a
better fit for how athletes and coaches actually talk about races.

This is easiest to see in the review surfaces themselves.

`TODO: insert screenshot of the week review table with row-level feedback and clickable single-session review`

The weekly review flow:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Load saved weekly plan] --> B[Sync completed activities from Intervals.icu]
    B --> C[Attach wellness rows from Intervals.icu]
    C --> D[User edits row-level feedback]
    D --> E[Deterministic weekly compliance summaries]
    E --> F[Retrieve coaching evidence from vector store]
    F --> G[OpenAI generates weekly coach review]
    G --> H[Save weekly review state + coach review to GCS]
```

And the narrower single-session review flow:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[User opens one completed session] --> B[Fetch activity detail from Intervals.icu]
    B --> C[Deterministic analysis<br/>session identity, structure match, rep match, intensity execution, HR, compliance bands]
    C --> D[Retrieve coaching evidence]
    D --> E[OpenAI generates session feedback]
    E --> F[Store review payload in weekly review state on GCS]
```

That deterministic layer is much richer now than it was in the early review
versions. The app does not just compute a generic compliance percentage and ask
the model to improvise a judgment. It first builds a structured session-match
object that separates:

- whether the right sport and rough session volume happened
- whether the macro structure matched the prescription
- whether the repeated work matched at rep level
- whether the key work intervals were on target, harder, or easier

That distinction turned out to matter a lot. A session can match the intended
structure while still running slightly harder than prescribed, and those are
not the same coaching message. The UI now exposes that deterministic analysis
back to the user through summary cards, a block-match table, and an intensity
evidence table instead of hiding it inside the prompt payload.

### Model selection became task-specific

Another important refinement is that the system no longer assumes one model
should handle every task.

That was acceptable early on, but it is not a very good operational policy.
Season planning has the broadest context window, the highest consequence of bad
reasoning, and now includes a two-pass clarification loop. Single-session
feedback is much narrower. Repair passes are narrower again. Treating all of
those as the same LLM problem is convenient in code, but not very disciplined.

The current app routes models by request type:

- season planning uses the strongest model
- weekly planning uses a strong but cheaper model
- weekly-plan repair uses a smaller model
- weekly review uses a smaller model
- single-session feedback uses a smaller model

This is configured explicitly rather than buried in prompt code, and the
telemetry records the resolved model plus aggregate `models_used` for each run.
That matters because one logical workflow can now be mixed-model: a weekly plan
run may start with one model and use a cheaper one for repair. The monitoring
surface therefore has to cost runs from run-level usage logs, not by assuming
one model everywhere.

### Compliance interpretation moved out of the model

Early versions of the review workflow passed raw compliance percentages into
the model and let it decide what they meant. That turned out to be too loose.
A one-percent miss in duration or load could trigger negative commentary even
when the deviation was operationally meaningless. In simple terms, I was getting
feedback like this:

>> You cut today run short. This could be because of accumulated fatigue, even you
>> marked it as "felt easy and realexed pace all the way through". We will need to
>> adjust the training load next week.

How much did I cut the session short? I made a 90min run an 88min one. Unforgivable...

Whether a deviation is trivial, minor, or significant is not the kind of thing
that should be rediscovered probabilistically on every run. It is a policy
decision, and policy decisions are better encoded deterministically.

The current system now computes explicit compliance bands before the coach sees
the data, and it interprets them together with the structured session-match
object rather than as isolated percentages.

For single-session review, the app computes:

- signed duration and load deltas
- explicit over-versus-under compliance (i.e. cutting 10min, or adding 10min?)
- tolerance-aware labels such as `ignore`, `minor`, `moderate`, and `major`
- absolute guardrails so a tiny miss in minutes or load is not treated as
  meaningful just because the session was short

The current thresholds are intentionally simple:

- less than 5% can be ignored
- 5% to 10% is minor
- 10% to 30% is moderate
- 30% or more is significant

This means the model no longer has to decide from scratch whether 99% versus
101% compliance deserves criticism. The software tells it directly that those
cases are inside tolerance unless something else in the workout strongly
contradicts that interpretation. It also means that missing the power target
on a key threshold rep is treated very differently from riding a cooldown a bit
too hard. Warmup, cooldown, and recovery still matter, but they no longer
automatically flip the whole session verdict if the key work was executed
correctly.

At the weekly review level, the same idea is aggregated rather than repeated
row by row. The coach now sees pattern summaries such as:

- share of sessions within tolerance
- average signed load and duration delta
- counts of over- and under-execution
- count of major deviations

That is much closer to how a human coach would think. A weekly review should
focus on patterns, not on nitpicking every minor discrepancy. If most sessions
were within tolerance and only one session drifted by a few percent, that is
not an insight. It is noise.

This is a good example of the broader design direction. The model still writes
the coaching interpretation, but the application is increasingly responsible
for deciding what deserves interpretation in the first place.

## How data is organized in GCS

One of the more consequential changes was not the UI. It was deciding to make
GCS the durable backing store and to be explicit about how data is laid out
there.

At a high level, the bucket stores a mix of:

- normalized parquet tables for analytical and cross-surface reads
- JSON artifacts for workflow state and model inputs/outputs
- JSONL logs for observability

The layout is intentionally simple and path-based.

Example structure:

```text
training_automation/
  clubs/{club_id}/
    metadata/
      tenancy/*.parquet
    coaches/{coach_id}/
      metadata/coach.json
      athletes/{athlete_id}/
        metadata/
          active_season.json
          catalog.json
          week_plan/{season_id}/{week_start}.json
          week_review/{season_id}/{week_start}.json
          weekly_review_output/{season_id}/{week_start}.json
          weekly_wellness/{season_id}/{week_start}.json
          zones_state.json
        tables/
          season_summary/season_id=.../part-000.parquet
          races/season_id=.../part-000.parquet
          season_blocks/season_id=.../part-000.parquet
          block_weekly_targets/season_id=.../part-000.parquet
          weekly_plan/season_id=.../part-000.parquet
          weekly_review/season_id=.../part-000.parquet
          athlete_profile/season_id=.../part-000.parquet
          athlete_settings/season_id=.../part-000.parquet
        artifacts/
          season_plans/{season_id}/latest/*.json
          season_plans/{season_id}/versions/{version_id}/*.json
  logs/
    llm_usage_events/YYYY/MM/DD/*.jsonl
    openai_usage_log/YYYY/MM/DD/*.jsonl
```

This split reflects two different access patterns.

The parquet tables are useful when the application wants normalized relational
reads. For example:

- load all races for one season
- query projected fitness rows
- inspect weekly review history
- reconstruct planner defaults from persisted season tables

The JSON artifacts are useful when the workflow needs to preserve a richer
object exactly as it existed at one step in the process. For example:

- a generated week plan payload before it is flattened into a table
- the saved state of the editable week review surface
- the full season-planning bundle and its versioned artifacts
- generated coach-review outputs

That combination turned out to be more practical than trying to force
everything into either tables only or JSON only.

### Why this structure instead of a traditional relational database?

There are several reasons.

First, the workflow is artifact-heavy.

The application does not only manage transactional entities like sessions or
races. It also manages generated bundles, previews, editable workflow state,
versioned plan artifacts, and telemetry payloads. Those objects are often more
naturally stored as files than as rows spread across many normalized tables.

Second, read patterns are narrow and seasonal.

This is not a high-concurrency product with many simultaneous users mutating
shared records. It is a constrained single-athlete workflow with a small set of
known reads:

- load one active season
- load one saved week
- load one weekly review state
- load one set of artifacts for inspection

For that pattern, object storage plus cached parquet reads is often simpler
than running and maintaining a database service.

Third, versioning and auditability are easier.

A versioned season plan bundle in object storage is straightforward to persist
and inspect. Keeping both a `latest/` pointer and explicit
`versions/{version_id}/` directories makes it easy to answer questions like:

- what exactly did the model produce?
- what inputs were used?
- what was later confirmed?

That is possible in a relational database too, but it usually requires more
schema design up front and more care around immutable historical records.

Fourth, the app already lives in a file-oriented world.

Prompt assets, JSON schemas, deployment files, and logs are all file-like
artifacts. Storing workflow state in a compatible medium keeps the system
conceptually simpler.

### Why parquet and JSON specifically?

Parquet is used for normalized tables because:

- it is compact
- it reads efficiently through DuckDB
- it preserves typed columns better than ad hoc CSV
- it is convenient for analytical inspection later

JSON is used for workflow state and generated artifacts because:

- it preserves the original nested structure
- it is easy to diff and inspect manually
- it maps naturally to LLM inputs and outputs
- it avoids impedance mismatch for state that is not naturally tabular

In other words, the storage layer is not trying to pretend every object has
the same shape. Some parts of the workflow are relational, and some are
artifact-shaped. The GCS layout accepts that directly.

## Storage and deployment changed the reliability profile

### Durable storage reduced ambiguity

The app now persists:

- season plans and related artifacts
- weekly plan payloads
- weekly review state
- generated weekly coach reviews
- wellness snapshots
- zones state and active-season metadata

This gives the workflow a real memory that is separate from the browser
session and separate from any one downstream table.

That is important for two reasons.

First, it makes recovery much cleaner. Reopening the app can reuse saved
artifacts rather than reconstructing everything from scratch.

Second, it improves auditability. When something looks wrong, there is an
actual stored payload to inspect rather than only the latest UI state.

### Cloud Run made the runtime model simpler

Deploying to Google Cloud Run also tightened the system boundary.

The app is now a hosted runtime with:

- server-side secrets from Secret Manager
- a stable deployment script
- public access gated by a lightweight app password
- cloud-hosted persistence in the same operational environment

This does not magically make the system production-grade in every respect. The
current password gate is still an MVP access control mechanism, not strong
authentication.

But it does solve a real engineering problem: the system is now usable as a
single deployed application from anywhere in the world, rather than as a local
development workflow that happens to call APIs.

## Retrieval and observability improved the LLM layer

### Retrieval is now an enforced dependency

Another meaningful change is the use of live OpenAI vector-store retrieval as
the evidence source for generation surfaces.

This addresses a
specific problem: the stable instruction file is necessary, but it is not a
complete coaching knowledge base.

The system now expects generation to be grounded in retrieved evidence rather
than in whatever the base model happens to remember. The important design
point is that retrieval failure is handled conservatively. If no evidence is
returned, generation fails closed rather than silently degrading into
ungrounded output.

A retrieval-backed system that silently proceeds when retrieval breaks is only
pretending to be retrieval-backed.

The retival store was built by embedding knowledge from books by Joe Friel and 
Matt Fitzgerald, among others. Note that this is copyrighted material. I am OK using
it for this PoC, as I purchesed the books myself and it is only for my personal use,
but if you plan to commercialize solutions like this you need to be careful not to
infringe any Copyright law.

### Retrieval is now structured, not just present

The first retrieval-backed version still had a weakness: although the model was
given external evidence, the evidence store itself was too coarse. Most of the
source material was uploaded at the whole-book level. That meant the retriever
could find the right author or the right book but still return the wrong
abstraction level. A season-planning query could easily surface swim stroke
mechanics, and a workout-feedback query could pull annual-periodization prose.

The current version fixes that by changing the corpus itself, not only the
prompt.

The books are now split into section-level files before upload, and each file
receives controlled metadata such as:

- planning level: macrocycle, mesocycle, microcycle, workout, technique, reference
- topic: season planning, weekly planning, taper, recovery, swim technique, session library, and so on
- sport: triathlon, duathlon, swim, bike, run, strength, or multi
- phase and distance focus where those distinctions are meaningful

That makes retrieval more like a real information system and less like generic
semantic similarity over a pile of long documents.

At runtime, the app now uses task-specific metadata filters:

- season planning biases toward macrocycle and mesocycle planning material
- weekly planning biases toward mesocycle, microcycle, and workout guidance
- single-session review biases toward workout and technique material

There is also a pragmatic safeguard here. Filtered retrieval is useful only if
the corpus is well tagged. So the app logs filtered retrieval, but if a
metadata-filtered search returns no hits it automatically retries the same query
without the task-level filters instead of failing for the wrong reason. In
other words, retrieval is stricter than before, but not brittle.

This is a small architectural point with a large practical effect. The quality
gain did not come from "better prompts" alone. It came from representing the
knowledge base in a way that matches the structure of the coaching problem.

### Cost monitoring becomes operational

The original workflow already logged token usage, but the current version has a
clearer observability split.

The most important addition is persistent telemetry written to GCS.

Detailed LLM usage and event logs now persist under date-partitioned paths, so
the system has a longer-lived usage history outside the current session. That
matters because it allows me to monitor costs and identify areas where the code
can be tightened rather than only tuning prompts.

This also matters for deterministic rules, not only for tokens. For example,
weekly planning now emits a dedicated `weekly_plan_load_rule` monitoring event
when the calculated load materially disagrees with a model-produced estimate,
or when a structured prescription is still too vague to score reliably. The
run-level logs also now record a `log_schema_version`, the plan generation
mode, structured-template candidate counts, how many intents were materialized
through deterministic templates versus generic fallback rows, grouped
materialization failure reasons, and a backward-compatible legacy-fallback
flag. That makes it possible to distinguish “the model was expensive”
from “the deterministic planner had to fall back because template coverage or
validation was insufficient.” The same run-level records now also distinguish
between three repair layers: deterministic patching, deterministic
re-materialization, and targeted LLM repair.

The same logic now applies to season planning. Because the season workflow is
two-pass, telemetry can distinguish the initial draft from the clarification
pass. That means I can inspect not only total season-planning cost, but whether
the system is getting cleaner first-pass plans over time or simply shifting
cost into the follow-up pass.

Now, questions like these become easier to answer:

- Which workflow surface is the main token consumer?
- How often does weekly planning require repair?
- Are single-session reviews cheap enough to be offered more broadly?
- Is latency drifting after prompt or retrieval changes?
- Are failures concentrated in retrieval, validation, storage writes, or
  deterministic template materialization misses?

## The workflow is now stricter in the right places

The most useful improvement is not any one feature. It is the cumulative
effect of several stricter boundaries.

- The form layer rejects obviously invalid inputs earlier.
- The UI separates generation, confirmation, editing, and saving into distinct
  steps.
- Storage provides durable state instead of relying on transient app memory.
- Monitoring exposes token and request behavior as an engineering signal.
- Weekly planning now separates intent generation from deterministic workout
  materialization, which is a much better boundary than asking the model to
  invent every interval structure from scratch.

The point is to make the non-deterministic component live inside a workflow
that is more stateful, inspectable, and recoverable than the first version,
while leveraging GenAI to flexibly generate plans and provide insights.

## Tradeoffs

The newer design is better, but it is not free.

- the application is more complex than the original script-oriented workflow
- storage, deployment, and retrieval introduce more moving parts
- UI code creates another maintenance surface in addition to prompts and
  orchestration logic
- cloud persistence and monitoring improve operability, but they also make the
  system more infrastructure-dependent

Those tradeoffs are acceptable because they buy control in the places where
the original version was weakest: input handling, state continuity, and
operational visibility.

## Conclusion

The first version of this coaching system answered a design question: can an
LLM-assisted training workflow be made repeatable with normalized state,
validation, and repair?

The current version answers a different question: what changes when that
workflow becomes an application?

The answer is that the important improvements are mostly outside the model.
They are input validation, explicit workflow surfaces, persistent storage,
retrieval discipline, deployable runtime boundaries, and usable observability.

That is the direction I currently find most convincing for applied LLM
systems. The quality of generation still matters, but once the basic workflow
works, the bigger engineering gains come from making the system easier to
control.
